articles.title: Notícias g1 Centro-Oeste: Ciclista, Ana Elisa e acidente na MG-252 | G1
articles.standfirst: Resumo de notícias da semana entre os dias 10 a 16 de outubro.
articles.summary: As notícias g1 Centro-Oeste de Minas destacam o resgate de um cão por ciclista, ataques à deputada Ana Elisa e o trágico acidente fatal na MG-252.
articles.body:
Confira o que foi destaque no g1 Centro-Oeste nesta semana, com as notícias mais acessadas entre os dias 10 e 16 de outubro.

O que seria apenas mais um trecho de uma viagem de bicicleta pelo Cerrado brasileiro teve uma parada inesperada e ganhou um novo companheiro de caminho. O ciclista João Carlos Vieira, conhecido como Jotta Vieira, de Pedra do Indaiá , no Centro-Oeste de Minas Gerais, encontrou um cachorro abandonado sob uma temperatura de cerca de 37 ºC e com sede.

O encontro ocorreu no sábado (11), por volta das 14h, enquanto o ciclista pedalava por uma estrada de terra em Goiás.

Sem hesitar, Jotta parou para ajudar o animal e seguiu por cerca de 5 quilômetros com ele no colo até Santo Antônio de Goiás, onde conseguiu um novo tutor para o cão. Veja no vídeo acima o momento em que ele mata a sede do animal.

Deputada federal mais jovem eleita por Minas Gerais, Ana Elisa Santos Silva (PT), de 21 anos, desativou uma conta na rede social X, antigo Twitter, após receber ameaças de morte e de estupro. A decisão foi tomada na noite de quinta-feira (8), quando os ataques se intensificaram nas redes sociais, segundo a deputada eleita.

Por meio de um vídeo publicado no Instagram, Ana Elisa afirmou que as ameaças chegavam a cada dois minutos.

"Eu acredito que ninguém mereça sofrer ameaça de morte por estar politicamente engajado e tentando defender o que acha melhor para o país. O debate político para mim nunca foi sobre isso. A minha equipe desativou a minha conta no Twitter porque nós estávamos recebendo ameaça de morte a cada dois minutos. Ameaça de morte e ameaça de estupro", disse a jovem.

Jonas e Cristiane — Foto: Redes sociais/Reprodução

Jonas Jolvery Aguiar Silva, de 36 anos, e Cristiane Maria Silva Nunes, de 28 anos, morreram em um acidente de carro na MG-252, em Perdigão no domingo (11). Os corpos do casal foram sepultados na segunda-feira (12), no Cemitério Municipal de Araújos .

O filho do casal, de nove meses, também estava no carro e ficou ferido. Ele foi socorrido e levado ao pronto-socorro de Perdigão e, posteriormente, transferido para outra unidade de saúde. O nome do hospital e o estado de saúde do bebê não foram divulgados.

Jonas e Cristiane eram casados desde 2018 e moravam em Araújos. O casal teve o primeiro filho em 2026. O motorista envolvido no acidente é investigado por homicídio culposo .

articles.standfirst: Com investimento municipal, novo espaço de 6 mil m² na Ajuda de Cima garante opções completas de esporte e convivência para a Zona Norte.
articles.summary: Com investimento municipal, novo espaço de 6 mil m² na Ajuda de Cima garante opções completas de esporte e convivência para a Zona Norte.
articles.body:
Novo parque público no bairro Ajuda de Cima garante opções de esporte, lazer e convivência para todas as idades — Foto: Arquivo Secom

A Prefeitura de Macaé entregou à população o novo Parque Municipal Joventino de Souza (Nhô Manduca), localizado na Estrada Hildebrando Alves Barbosa, antiga Estrada do Imburo, na Ajuda de Cima. O espaço de lazer e convivência recebeu investimentos de R$ 4,1 milhões e atende a uma reivindicação histórica dos moradores da Zona Norte, oferecendo infraestrutura moderna de esporte e recreação para toda a família.

Com cerca de 6 mil metros quadrados de área total, o parque foi construído ao longo de 18 meses e conta com campo de futebol em grama sintética com arquibancada, playground infantil, quiosques, área de contemplação e banheiros. O equipamento público integra as ações do município para ampliação das áreas de lazer e melhoria da qualidade de vida nos bairros.

Pista de skate profissional Vanoni foi projetada para receber treinos e competições regionais — Foto: Arquivo Secom

Junto ao parque, a prefeitura inaugurou a Pista de Skate Profissional Vanoni, planejada com assessoria técnica especializada para atender skatistas locais e sediar futuros eventos esportivos estaduais e nacionais. A cerimônia de entrega reuniu autoridades municipais, lideranças comunitárias e familiares dos homenageados que dão nome ao parque e ao complexo esportivo.

A criação da praça e do espaço esportivo beneficia diretamente os moradores dos bairros Ajuda de Cima, Piracema, Jardim Franco, Itaparica, Vale Verde e Nova Esperança, garantindo aos jovens e crianças um local seguro para a prática esportiva e atividades ao ar livre perto de casa.

articles.title: 'Women ought to be released after sunset': Neha Bora questions night-long detentions over anti-SIR stir
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora on Saturday questioned the overnight detention of protesters, over the anti-SIR
articles.body: NEW DELHI: All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora on Saturday questioned the overnight detention of protesters, over the anti-SIR stir, saying women ought to be released after sunset and alleging that police denied her access to a lawyer for hours.Bora was detained under preventive provisions on the evening of October 16 and released early Saturday after formal procedures under Section 65 of the Delhi Police Act, Delhi Police said.“Under what authority is this justified? By what law or order is it permissible to keep detainees held in custody all night long? Legally, individuals, especially women, ought to be released after sunset, yet this is not happening,” Bora said.She alleged that police demanded her personal details but did not allow her to speak to or consult a lawyer for a long time. “Our lawyers spent 5–6 hours trying to reach me. It was only after we managed to call them that they were finally allowed to meet me,” she said.Bora also accused authorities of creating chaos in Central Delhi through roadblocks and restrictions, while questioning the police response to the protests."Law and order are being flouted in every possible way. Ordinary citizens are treated as if they were hardened criminals, a practice that has persisted in this country for a long time," she said."Furthermore, there is a new narrative being pushed, one of chaos and anarchy. What kind of chaos and anarchy? The one you unleashed in Central Delhi? The people of Delhi cannot even breathe a sigh of relief; whichever route they take to get to work, they find it blocked. You are spreading chaos and anarchy across the nation. Please, spare the people of India. Impeach Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR, so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured," she added.Calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s impeachment and a halt to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, she said the move was necessary to ensure citizens’ voting rights.Meanwhile, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was also detained on Friday evening ahead of the ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ protest, is set to be produced before a special executive magistrate court.Delhi Police said action under Sections 126 and 170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita was initiated against him.CJP had earlier alleged that Dipke was taken to an undisclosed location and denied access to lawyers, claiming his family and party members were unable to contact him for more than 10 hours. AISA had also said Bora’s whereabouts remained unknown for several hours before its lawyers traced her to the RK Puram police station around midnight.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Alberta separation vote: Why the oil-rich province wants to break away from Canada
articles.summary: Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta is heading into a crucial vote on whether to begin the legal process for a future referendum on independence, with
articles.body: Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta is heading into a crucial vote on whether to begin the legal process for a future referendum on independence, with Prime Minister Mark Carney warning that separation could trigger years of uncertainty and deepen divisions across the country.The vote, scheduled for Monday, is not a direct referendum on independence. Instead, voters will decide whether Alberta should remain a Canadian province or instruct the provincial government to begin the constitutional process required to hold a binding referendum on separation.The vote comes amid growing tensions between Alberta and the federal government over energy policies, provincial autonomy and the distribution of economic benefits. The province's long-running sense of alienation from Ottawa has fuelled the separatist movement, which argues that federal policies have constrained Alberta's oil and gas industry and limited its control over its resources.However, polling suggests that outright support for separation remains a minority position, with most Albertans favouring remaining in Canada.Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, has made a last-minute appeal for unity, warning that the vote comes at a particularly dangerous time as US President Donald Trump wages a trade war against Canada and repeatedly threatens to make the country the 51st US state.“This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Calgary on Thursday. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.”The prime minister urged Albertans not to use the vote simply to send a message to Ottawa, warning that a vote against Canada could lead to prolonged political and economic uncertainty.“Don't be fooled by the idea you can send a message' with your vote,” Carney said. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.”Why does Alberta want to separate from Canada?Alberta's separatist movement is rooted in what is commonly known as "western alienation", a longstanding sentiment among some residents of Canada's western provinces that federal politicians in Ottawa overlook their interests and give them inadequate influence over national policy.The province is home to most of Canada's proven oil reserves and has one of the country's most resource-dependent economies. Many separatists argue that federal environmental regulations, energy policies and restrictions on pipeline development have prevented Alberta from fully benefiting from its oil and gas wealth.They also contend that Alberta contributes more to federal revenues than it receives in return and that Ottawa exercises excessive control over the province's internal affairs.The movement gained momentum following the COVID-19 pandemic, when some activists who had organised against vaccine mandates and other public health restrictions turned their attention to independence. The 2022 Freedom Convoy protests against pandemic restrictions also helped some activists build political networks and mobilise supporters.The separatist campaign subsequently gathered enough momentum to push the question of independence into mainstream provincial politics.Earlier this year, an independence petition attracted more than 300,000 signatures. However, an Alberta court blocked the proposed citizen-led referendum after ruling that the province had failed to consult Indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected by separation.Premier Danielle Smith criticised the ruling and argued that the issue could not be postponed indefinitely. Her government appealed against the decision, while separatists continued to press for a vote.An opposing campaign, Forever Canadian, has also attracted considerable support, collecting more than 400,000 signatures from Albertans who want the province to remain part of Canada.What will Albertans vote on?The referendum is not a straightforward choice between independence and remaining in Canada. Instead, the ballot asks voters whether Alberta should stay a province or begin the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding referendum on separation.A vote in favour of beginning that process would therefore not automatically make Alberta independent. It would initiate another stage of legal and political proceedings before residents could vote directly on whether to leave Canada.The ballot also contains nine other questions, largely focused on immigration, constitutional arrangements and provincial powers. These include proposals for greater provincial control over immigration, restrictions on access to certain public services for non-permanent residents, proof-of-citizenship requirements for provincial elections, and changes to the selection of provincial judges and senators.Smith has supported holding the vote despite opposing independence herself. She has argued that Albertans have legitimate grievances against Ottawa but that the province can secure greater autonomy while remaining part of Canada.“Canada can still work,” Smith said after voting on Wednesday. “We just need to make some changes.”Carney and Smith unite against separationCarney has made Alberta's continued membership of Canada a central part of his campaign, seeking to reassure residents that the federal government's approach to energy policy has changed.His government has moved to improve relations with Alberta, including fast-tracking a proposed oil pipeline to the Pacific. Carney has presented the project as a way to expand energy exports, create jobs and reduce Canada's dependence on the United States.The prime minister has also acknowledged the province's longstanding frustration with federal policies.“The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” he said, recalling how Ottawa had made residents feel “like our resources weren't our own”.Smith, meanwhile, has pointed to agreements with Carney's government as evidence that Alberta can secure concessions without breaking away. She has said the federal government has addressed seven of nine laws opposed by her province and cited cooperation over the proposed pipeline.The two leaders appeared together in Red Deer on Friday in a show of unity against separation. Smith praised the improved relationship with Ottawa, while Carney appealed to voters to preserve national unity.Federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, Carney's main political rival, has also urged Albertans to remain in Canada.“Don't leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said.However, separatist leaders remain unconvinced that the agreements will resolve their concerns. Tanya Clemens, co-chair of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, described the arrangements as “pinky promises” that did not adequately address the province's grievances.Clemens and other campaigners argue that Alberta needs greater control over its resources and economic future, with some viewing independence as the ultimate objective and others seeing the threat of separation as leverage in negotiations with Ottawa.How much support does Alberta's independence movement have?Polling indicates that most Albertans want to remain part of Canada, suggesting that the campaign for independence faces a substantial hurdle.A Leger poll published earlier this month found that 70% of respondents wanted Alberta to remain as it is, while just over 20% supported beginning the legal process for a future binding referendum. Around 7% were undecided.A September survey by Janet Brown Opinion Research for CBC found that 72% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who favoured moving towards separation. Support for independence was relatively higher among male and rural voters.Smith has previously said that even support of around 22% for separation was too high for her liking.Despite the apparent majority in favour of remaining in Canada, the vote carries political risks. Some residents may support moving towards a separation referendum not because they necessarily want independence, but because they want to register their dissatisfaction with the federal government.This possibility has prompted concerns about a surprise outcome similar to Britain's 2016 Brexit referendum, when voters chose to leave the European Union despite expectations that the Remain campaign would prevail. However, the available polling suggests that such an outcome in Alberta is unlikely.Who is leading the separatist campaign?The independence movement has been driven by activists including Mitch Sylvestre, a businessman from Bonnyville, and Calgary-based lawyer Jeffrey Rath, both associated with the Alberta Prosperity Project.The group argues that years of federal Liberal rule have undermined Alberta's economic interests, particularly through policies affecting oil production, pipeline development and resource exports.Some separatists have also explored the possibility of closer ties with the United States. Rath has travelled to Washington on what he described as fact-finding missions, during which separatists sought to understand whether the US government would support an independent Alberta with a line of credit.However, the movement is not united on what independence should look like. Some supporters want Alberta to become a fully independent country, while others view the campaign as a way to force Ottawa to grant the province greater autonomy. A smaller number have expressed openness to joining the United States.The movement has also created political pressure for Smith, who faces separatist activists within her own United Conservative Party even as she campaigns for Alberta to remain in Canada.What happens if Albertans vote for separation?A vote in favour of beginning the legal process would not immediately trigger independence. Instead, it would set the stage for further constitutional and legal steps, potentially leading to a binding referendum as early as 2027, according to Smith.Any eventual attempt to separate would raise complex constitutional questions, including negotiations with the federal government and other provinces, as well as issues involving Indigenous rights, territorial boundaries, public debt, natural resources and the division of government assets.The court's earlier ruling on Indigenous consultation has already demonstrated one of the legal challenges facing the movement.A vote to remain in Canada would weaken the immediate push for separation, although it would not necessarily eliminate the grievances that have sustained the movement.For now, the central question is whether Albertans want to take the first formal step towards a possible break with Canada or use the vote to demand changes while remaining part of the federation. With polling indicating that most residents favour staying, independence appears unlikely in the near term, but the referendum could reshape Alberta's relationship with Ottawa regardless of the outcome.You use AI every day. articles.title: 202,000 cases, 1,147 deaths: Bangladesh battles deadly measles outbreak amid warning to other nations
articles.summary: Bangladesh is struggling to contain what has emerged as the worst measles outbreak this year, with more than 1,100 deaths reported amid falling
articles.body: Bangladesh is struggling to contain what has emerged as the worst measles outbreak this year, with more than 1,100 deaths reported amid falling vaccination coverage, gaps in healthcare outreach and weaknesses in official data, according to a Reuters report.The country reported 202,000 suspected measles cases, including 22,000 laboratory-confirmed infections, between the outbreak’s start in mid-March and October 9, the World Health Organization (WHO) said. At least 1,147 people have died, with children under five accounting for 94% of reported deaths.“This is a real warning to every country,” Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at New York University’s School of Global Public Health, told Reuters, stressing that preventing outbreaks through vaccination is easier, cheaper and safer than responding to a crisis.Vaccination coverage falls below critical thresholdBangladesh’s response was hampered by incomplete data on children, inadequate preparation for emergency vaccination and difficulties reaching parents in remote communities.WHO and UNICEF estimated that in 2024, the country achieved 96% coverage for the first measles vaccine dose and 93% for the second.However, vaccination coverage declined amid political turmoil following the protests that ended former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s 15-year rule in 2024. Health workers went on strike, vaccine orders were delayed and follow-up vaccinations were disrupted, Reuters reported.A WHO-UNICEF report published in July estimated that first-dose coverage fell to 90% in 2025, while second-dose coverage dropped to 86%. Both figures were below the 95% coverage the WHO says is necessary to prevent outbreaks.Emergency vaccination drive missed millions of childrenBangladesh launched an emergency vaccination campaign in April and May, with nearly 20 million children receiving a dose. The government initially said the campaign had covered all children aged six months to five years.However, a subsequent routine health intervention in June had a target list containing four million more children in the same age group, exposing a significant gap in the emergency campaign’s reach, according to Reuters.By August, the proportion of children with confirmed measles who had not been vaccinated remained virtually unchanged, rising from 82% before the campaign to 85% afterwards, meeting documents reviewed by Reuters showed.“When preparedness checks are not done properly, it is often the poorest and hardest-to-reach children who miss out on vaccination and pay the price,” Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and chair of Bangladesh’s National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination, told Reuters.You use AI every day. articles.body: Iran is facing mounting financial pressure after nine months of war, with a US naval blockade costing it $25 billion in lost oil revenue and $350 million in cryptocurrency frozen, according to US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Adm Brad Cooper.In a video message released on Friday, Cooper said Iran-backed groups across the region, including Hezbollah, Hamas and Shia militias in Iraq, were sending money back to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which has funded them for years."The financial strain on Iran's military has become so significant that there are reports about Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments for their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also isn't paying its troops," Cooper said.He added that the Iranian government was withholding salaries, pensions and benefits from public sector workers, including internal security personnel and members of the IRGC.The financial squeeze comes as the Trump administration maintains a naval blockade and sanctions on Iran, hoping to push Tehran towards a deal that includes concessions on its nuclear programme. However, Iran has yet to respond to a US counterproposal aimed at ending the war.Cooper said CENTCOM and the US Treasury Department had also frozen $350 million in Iranian cryptocurrency in recent weeks. The naval blockade, meanwhile, had cost Tehran $25 billion in lost oil revenue, he said.Strait of Hormuz tensionsCooper attributed the recent increase in Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz to what he described as desperation within the IRGC.Despite the attacks, the strategic waterway remains open, he said, with 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moving through it over the past week.The US military has largely paused strikes on Iranian anti-ship missiles and attack drone launchers around the strait in recent weeks. A US official said the White House ordered the pause to avoid escalating the conflict ahead of the November midterm elections.US officials are concerned that continued attacks could discourage shipping companies from using the strait, reducing oil supplies and pushing up global prices. They also believe Iran is seeking to raise oil prices and increase pressure on US President Donald Trump ahead of the elections.Meanwhile, the White House and Qatari mediators are awaiting Tehran's response to Washington's counterproposal to end the war. A US official said the proposal was still under consideration in Tehran.Regional mediators have urged Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi not to delay the response until after the midterm elections, warning that there is no guarantee Trump would take a more conciliatory approach afterwards.You use AI every day. articles.title: Australian designer Joost Bakker built a three-storey urban farm home at Melbourne's Federation Square that produced its own food and power
articles.summary: A house in the middle of Melbourne that grew its own food, generated its own power and turned human waste into cooking gas.
articles.body: A house in the middle of Melbourne that grew its own food, generated its own power and turned human waste into cooking gas. That was Future Food System, a three-storey urban farm built by Dutch-born, Australian-raised designer Joost Bakker at Federation Square. Chefs lived inside, cooking only with what the building produced, from aquaponic trout to crickets and mushrooms. A feature documentary later followed the project from construction to pack-down. This article explains how the house worked, what it was made from, and why architects, restaurateurs and ordinary readers are still paying attention to its ideas for greener cities.Why Joost Bakker says eating is among humanity's most destructive acts and built a house in responseJoost Bakker did not set out to design an ordinary house. Writing for the Guardian, Max Veenhuyzen describes him as a Dutch-born, Australian-raised designer and no-waste advocate who has long been something of a provocateur, with a past that includes flower arrangements built from electrical clamps and steel frames, hay-bale restaurants with rooftop gardens, and bones from fine-diners boiled up and served at a soup kitchen. The film Greenhouse by Joost opens with his blunt view: "The most destructive things we humans do," Bakker says, "is eat." According to The Guardian, two decades of high-concept sustainability projects came to a head in 2020, when Bakker began construction of Future Food System, an off-grid house that produced all of its own power and food.Cooking gas from human waste, solar panels, and thirty-five tonnes of soil: how the house ran itselfEven the cooking gas came from human and food waste, thanks to a biodigester toilet. Gourmet Traveller explains that the biodigester turned toilet and organic waste into methane for the kitchen stoves, as well as compost, while solar panels, a recyclable battery system and rainwater tanks supported the rest of the house. Flora and Fauna adds that Australian solar panels clad the exterior and fed a nickel-iron battery wall. The Guardian also notes that the foundation-less building was anchored by self-watering garden beds filled with thirty-five tonnes of soil, showing that the gardens were part of the structure rather than decoration.Crickets, aquaponic trout and shower-grown mushrooms: How two live-in chefs ate only on-site produceFood came from the building itself. The Guardian reports that Jo Barrett and Matt Stone, Bakker's business partners and the house's live-in cooks, fed themselves and guests with produce grown on-site, including falafel-type balls enriched with crickets, an ice-cream analogue made with tiger nut milk, and marron, yabbies and trout raised aquaponically. Gourmet Traveller adds freshwater mussels, barramundi, a worm farm, a couple of chickens for eggs and an urban beehive. Steam from the showers grew mushrooms, a design detail turning bathroom humidity into a habitat for mycelium. The limited larder was challenging, yet the chefs call the experience rewarding. Barrett told the Guardian that her time at the house developed her more as a chef than her entire previous cooking career.Straw panels from Bendigo, natural lime and recycled concrete tiles, the non-toxic materials it usedDurra Panel, a biodegradable, fireproof wall and ceiling panel made of straw at a factory in Bendigo. Breathe says Bakker worked with local fabricators, agroforestry timber suppliers and sawmills so every material was sustainable, reusable and healthy for human habitation. The Design Files notes that the tiles were recycled concrete that can be recycled again, while Gourmet Traveller adds furniture made from a single cypress tree and recyclable polypropylene pipes. Together, these choices aimed to keep the building healthy for the people living inside.How architects, restaurateurs and a documentary carried Bakker's ideas well beyond Federation SquareThe project also shaped how professionals think. The Guardian reports that Jeremy McCloud, co-founder of the Melbourne architecture firm Breathe, has received client requests for rooftop gardens and Durra Panel, and he told the Guardian that Bakker holds aspirational conversations with developers and governments that architects cannot. The restaurant business Trader House Group hired Bakker in January 2022 as a consultant to tackle waste. Breathe says the structure stood at Federation Square from January 2021 to June 2022 before being relocated as the next home for Bakker's mother. Bakker said that houses covered with plants, ecosystems and waterfalls are possible without harming the planet, and the documentary reached Victorian cinemas on 10 November 2022.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Prioritize rights & freedoms when you meet Indian officials': US lawmakers urge Marco Rubio amid anti-SIR stir
articles.summary: US lawmakers have urged secretary of state Marco Rubio to raise concerns over democratic freedoms with Indian officials during his upcoming visit.
articles.body: US lawmakers have urged secretary of state Marco Rubio to raise concerns over democratic freedoms with Indian officials during his upcoming visit.In a letter dated October 16, six US lawmakers, including Pramila Jayapal and James P McGovern, have urged Rubio to discuss freedom of expression, the right to protest and voting rights with Indian officials. They also raised concerns over student protests following exam-related issues and the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The lawmakers also noted steps taken by the government to address students' concerns, including education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.Jayapal reiterates call for freedom of expressionJayapal shared the appeal in a post on X on Friday (local time), stressing the responsibility of both countries to uphold democratic freedoms. “As the world’s largest democracies, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression.”“@RepMcGovern and I are urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to prioritize those freedoms and human rights when he meets with Indian officials in the coming days,” she added.The letter was signed by Jayapal, McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Chuy Garcia, Eleanor Holmes Norton and Ilhan Omar. It highlighted the importance of democratic principles in relations between the two countries.“As the world’s largest democracies and state parties to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression,” the letter stated.Student protests and voter roll revision flaggedThe lawmakers referred to protests following the leak and cancellation of the national medical college entrance examination. They also raised concerns over demonstrations linked to the Election Commission's SIR exercise.Citing concerns raised by UN human rights experts, the letter questioned the transparency of the voter roll revision process and its potential implications for electoral participation. It also referred to reports of protest-related detentions and the response of law enforcement agencies to demonstrations.The lawmakers acknowledged the Indian government's response to student grievances following examination-related concerns.“We note that the Indian government has taken some steps to address the grievances of students impacted by exam leaks, with the notable inclusion of Education Minister Pradhan’s resignation,” the letter stated.US lawmakers seek probe into demonstrationsThe letter also referred to reports that individuals associated with Indian diplomatic missions had photographed participants at demonstrations in Washington, Chicago and San Francisco. The lawmakers called for the reports to be investigated.They urged the US administration to encourage transparent investigations into alleged violations linked to law enforcement actions during protests, review detentions involving the exercise of fundamental freedoms and examine the reports concerning demonstrations in the United States.“The free exercise of fundamental freedoms and the right to vote is core to the democratic identities of both the United States and India,” the letter stated.The lawmakers called on Rubio to raise these issues during his meetings with Indian officials.India rejects Jayapal's remarksThe appeal comes after India strongly criticised Jayapal's comments on its electoral process on Friday, describing them as "unwarranted, uninformed" and tantamount to interference in the electoral practices of a fellow democracy.Responding to a question during a bi-weekly media briefing in New Delhi, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, "We find the remarks of the Congresswoman unwarranted and uninformed and tantamount to interfering in the electoral practices of a fellow democracy. This is an approach that undermines democracy itself."Earlier, on Thursday, India's Ambassador to the US, Vinay Mohan Kwatra, had also rejected Jayapal's allegations regarding a voter purge.Describing her remarks as "unacceptable interference in India's internal affairs", Kwatra wrote on X, "The remarks by Rep. Jayapal on India's electoral and political processes are unacceptable interference in India's internal affairs."He added, "India is a vibrant democracy with robust, independent constitutional institutions and a longstanding record of free and fair elections. Always open to constructive conversation with the Congresswoman to dispel her misconceptions."Rubio is scheduled to visit India and Uzbekistan between October 17 and 22. His India itinerary includes Mumbai and Jamnagar, where he is expected to meet senior Indian government officials to strengthen the bilateral strategic partnership and explore enhanced energy cooperation.Meanwhile, the ECI is conducting a nationwide Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in multiple phases. The Commission has clarified that lists identifying absent, shifted, deceased and duplicate voters were publicly displayed and shared with political parties. It has also maintained that people whose names have been deleted from the electoral rolls can apply for enrolment at any time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Verify before she vilifies': India rejects UN rapporteur's claims on youth protests
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India has rejected allegations by UN special rapporteur Gina Romero that young people in the country face retaliation and stigmatisation for
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India has rejected allegations by UN special rapporteur Gina Romero that young people in the country face retaliation and stigmatisation for discussing mental health and gender justice, calling the claims based on anonymous and unverified submissions.Speaking at an interactive dialogue with Romero during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee, India’s first secretary Anuj Swarup questioned the evidence cited in her report on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and association.“Yet, the special rapporteur, Ms Gina Romero, asserts that young people in India face retaliation or stigmatisation for discussing mental health or gender justice, though merely citing unnamed submissions in the footnote. This level of arbitrary report writing is precisely the reason that the United Nations and its institutions have lost credibility,” Swarup said.“A sweeping charge against the world's largest youth population resting on anonymous and unverified claims is not evidence. It is hearsay, dressed up as a UN report, and my delegation rejects it outright,” he added.Swarup said India’s Constitution guarantees freedom of assembly, association, speech and expression under Article 19, with these rights protected by an independent judiciary, a free press and the National Human Rights Commission.He also cited young people’s participation in political movements and engagement with senior government leaders as evidence of civic space in the country.“In which repressive state does a satirical youth party question the government, marches on the capital, and then sits across the table with senior national leaders?” he asked, referring to a youth-led political movement mentioned in Romero’s report.“Chair, a mandate holder who relies on anonymous inputs to generalise for 1.4 billion people does a disservice to the very mandate she holds. We urge this special rapporteur to verify before she vilifies and to bring the required rigour and fairness in her reports,” he said.The remarks come amid heightened scrutiny of the government’s handling of youth protests, including demonstrations over alleged irregularities in public examinations and the recent anti-SIR stir.Romero had alleged in posts on X on October 10 that peaceful youth protesters in India faced excessive force and arbitrary detention. She also claimed that more than 2,500 protesters had been sent to remote detention centres without legal support, with some allegedly tortured or sexually assaulted. She further alleged that phones had been seized, protest-related material deleted and internet access restricted.These allegations were made by Romero and were not independently established in the information provided by India’s statement.India, meanwhile, defended its response to student protests over examination irregularities, saying the government had engaged with young people and taken steps to address exam fraud.Swarup said Parliament had amended the Public Examinations Act, doubled punishments for paper leaks, overhauled the examination system and created fast-track courts in every state to prosecute exam fraud.He also pointed to the Viksit Bharat Young Leaders Dialogue, saying more than five million young people had participated this year and helped shape national priorities through direct engagement with the Prime Minister.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Washington parents built a hidden fairy garden between bookshelves for their daughters, filled with miniature trees and glowing stars
articles.summary: A couple in Washington has turned an unused corner of their home library into a hidden fairy garden, creating a special place filled with miniature trees,
articles.body: A couple in Washington has turned an unused corner of their home library into a hidden fairy garden, creating a special place filled with miniature trees, glowing stars and personal touches for their two young daughters. Melissa Miller, 41, and her husband, Aaron Miller, 38, designed the secret space to bring a little magic into their children's everyday lives. As reported by PEOPLE in an exclusive article published in August 2026, the project also reflects the couple's love of imaginative spaces and the importance of family memories.How did Washington parents create a hidden fairy garden for their daughtersThe idea began when the Millers moved into their home and discussed how to arrange the space for their family. According to PEOPLE, they asked their daughters, aged four and a half and eight, whether they would prefer separate bedrooms or a shared room alongside a family library. The girls chose the library, giving their parents an opportunity to create a reading space that would also encourage imagination.While Aaron was building the library, the couple noticed an empty area beneath some shelves in one corner. Rather than covering it completely, they decided to keep the space accessible for a future surprise. Melissa, who had loved stories about magical lands, hidden rooms and secret passages since childhood, felt that a fairy garden would suit the library's garden-inspired theme.The construction of the library took several months. However, the hidden garden did not take shape immediately. Melissa became occupied with another creative project, a dollhouse built into the wall, and temporarily forgot about the small corner she had set aside.A childhood dream found a place in the family homeMelissa eventually returned to the idea about two years after first discussing it with Aaron. As PEOPLE reports, she began making miniature trees and planning a tiny forest with a clearing where fairies could gather for a picnic.Her original plan was to complete the garden herself and let both daughters discover it when it was ready. However, her younger daughter was at home with her during the day, so Melissa eventually invited her to help with the surprise.The little girl was delighted to take part and enjoyed helping create something that her older sister could discover later. The project consequently became more than a decorative addition to the library. It also gave mother and daughter an opportunity to work together on a shared creative activity.Melissa's idea was closely connected to her own childhood wishes. She had always wanted to encounter something magical unexpectedly, rather than simply reading about it in a book. Creating a secret world inside her home allowed her to turn that long-held dream into something her daughters could experience themselves.What makes the miniature forest specialThe fairy garden's details were carefully made by hand. PEOPLE reports that Melissa used air-dry clay, paint and leftover artificial flowers and leaves from earlier projects to create several of the miniature trees. These materials helped her build a tiny woodland scene within the limited space beneath the bookshelves.The design includes a small clearing intended for a fairy picnic, bringing the idea of an enchanted forest into a compact corner of the library. The setting also features glowing stars, a moon and a little comet, adding a night-sky effect to the miniature landscape.One of the most difficult parts of the project was painting the inside of the awkwardly shaped space. Melissa told PEOPLE that reaching into the corner made the task particularly challenging. Nevertheless, she continued working until the scene was complete.The finished garden combines handmade decorations with elements chosen specifically for the family, making it different from a standard miniature display. Each detail contributes to a small world that reflects the children's interests and their parents' efforts to make the home feel full of surprises.The glowing stars honour a much-loved family memberBeyond its playful appearance, the fairy garden holds a deeply personal meaning for the Millers. The couple included details in memory of their son, Luke, who was stillborn in 2020.In her interview with PEOPLE, Melissa explained that the moon, stars and comet were added to remember him. Following Luke's death, the family spent considerable time healing and camping in nature. The summer of his death coincided with the appearance of Comet Neowise, which became a lasting reminder of him.The celestial decorations therefore serve a purpose beyond making the miniature forest look magical. They connect the family's experience of loss with memories of time spent outdoors and the process of healing together.By incorporating these elements into a place designed for their daughters, Melissa and Aaron created a space that brings together childhood wonder, family history and remembrance. The garden's meaning is personal, yet it remains part of an everyday setting where the girls can explore and play.Small figures reflect the daughters' individual personalitiesThe miniature characters also have personal connections. According to PEOPLE, a fairy sitting with an open book represents the older daughter, who enjoys reading and has a strong interest in learning and imaginative play. Melissa also described her interests in nature, gardening, animals, swimming and camping.The younger daughter is represented by a fairy on a swing, reflecting her love of swinging, jumping, art and creating little homes for her tiny toys. Her enthusiasm for helping with the garden made the figure especially fitting.Even the family's cat, Blossom, has a place in the miniature forest. Melissa added a small white cat with blue eyes to resemble the family's pet.These details make the display a reflection of the household rather than simply a decorative fairy scene. Each figure gives the girls something familiar to discover, while the hidden location adds another layer of excitement.A home filled with imaginative surprisesThe fairy garden is only one of several unusual features the Millers have created. PEOPLE reports that the family also has a Mouse House, a two-sided dollhouse built into a wall that opens into two different rooms. It includes electricity, tiny light switches and a working doorbell.Aaron has also built a saltwater fish tank into the living room wall, while the house features a secret passageway, fulfilling another of Melissa's childhood ambitions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Brazil's Amazon deforestation hits record low: Why it matters amid election battle
articles.summary: Brazil’s Amazon rainforest has recorded its lowest annual deforestation rate since records began in 1988, with 3,335 square kilometres of forest cleared
articles.body: Brazil’s Amazon rainforest has recorded its lowest annual deforestation rate since records began in 1988, with 3,335 square kilometres of forest cleared between August 2025 and July 2026, according to the country’s National Institute for Space Research (INPE).The area cleared was 41.8 per cent lower than the 5,731 square kilometres recorded in the previous 12-month period, marking a significant decline in forest loss.The figures offer a boost to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s efforts to curb deforestation and meet his government’s target of ending illegal forest clearance by 2030.The previous record low for Amazon deforestation was 4,571 square kilometres in 2011–12, while annual forest loss peaked at nearly 30,000 square kilometres in the mid-1990s.“This is an absolutely stratospheric drop … it’s like a dream,” environment minister João Paulo Capobianco said at a news conference in Brasília, according to Al Jazeera.Márcio Astrini, executive secretary of climate advocacy group Observatório do Clima, described the figures as a “historic achievement”, saying they demonstrated that political will could help curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions.The Brazilian Amazon lost an average of about 11,600 square kilometres of forest annually during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2019–2022 presidency, nearly 60 per cent more than the average in the preceding four years, Al Jazeera reported.Amazon deforestation becomes an election issueThe latest figures come ahead of Brazil’s October 25 presidential runoff between Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Polls have shown the two candidates neck and neck.Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to strengthen environmental oversight in the Amazon, prioritising areas facing the greatest pressure from deforestation and wildfires. His manifesto proposes focusing law enforcement on organised crime rather than extractive workers and small farmers.He has also praised his father’s opposition to what he describes as a “radical environmental agenda”. The election could therefore have implications for the future direction of Brazil’s environmental policy.Amazon, the lungs of the EarthOften described as the “lungs of the Earth”, the Amazon rainforest is one of the planet’s most important ecosystems, spanning approximately seven million square kilometres across South America.It plays a crucial role in regulating the global climate by absorbing carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and storing carbon in its trees, vegetation and soils.The Science Panel for the Amazon estimates that the region’s vegetation and soils store between 150 billion and 200 billion tonnes of carbon, making the protection of its forests significant for global efforts to limit climate change.The rainforest also helps regulate rainfall through evapotranspiration, a process in which trees absorb water from the soil and release moisture into the atmosphere. This moisture contributes to cloud formation and rainfall, sustaining the forest’s water cycle and influencing weather patterns across South America.According to the Science Panel for the Amazon’s assessment, the forest recycles a substantial proportion of its rainfall and releases moisture that travels through the atmosphere, sometimes described as “flying rivers”.The Amazon is also a major global biodiversity hotspot, supporting more than 10 per cent of known global biodiversity, including numerous species of plants and animals.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan has said that foreign-inspired terrorism has been largely contained in India, barring a few areas, while homegrown terrorism has nearly been eliminated."Homegrown terrorism has almost ended, while foreign-inspired terrorism is no longer visible in any other part of the country," he said.Speaking in Hyderabad, Mohan also identified narcotics, cybercrime and illegal immigration as key challenges facing Indian Police Service (IPS) trainees."Militant naxalism has come to an end; North East insurgency reduced to minuscule levels," he said.His remarks come amid a push by the Centre for stronger regional cooperation to combat terrorism and organised crime.Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Tuesday called on BIMSTEC member countries to strengthen cooperation against terrorism, disrupt terrorist financing and prevent terrorist networks from establishing safe havens in the region.Addressing the first Home Ministers’ Meeting of BIMSTEC countries in New Delhi, Shah said India follows a policy of “zero tolerance” towards terrorism and stressed the need for collective action to strengthen regional security.“Hosting the first BIMSTEC Home Ministers’ Meeting is a matter of great pride and fortune for India. BIMSTEC, in a way, has become an essential platform for regional integration, economic cooperation and collective security.With the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, India is going ahead today," Shah said.“We have always been committed to peace, coexistence and human welfare. We continue to be committed to these even today. India has never believed in attacking any country or establishing dominance over them. India has always believed in upholding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of every country and peaceful resolution of differences,” he added.Shah said trust among BIMSTEC members was strengthened by the understanding that each country's security arrangements should contribute to the security of others.He called for a collective commitment to ensure that terrorist networks could not find shelter, establish bases or training facilities, mobilise resources or carry out activities against other member countries.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In May 2020, four boys pulled a little girl from a powerful creek current; her mother’s reward was free burgers for life: “There is no amount of money that can ever be put on what you did”
articles.summary: TLDR: A little girl vanished beneath a bridge as rain-swollen Hubble Creek swept her into a dangerous culvert.
articles.body: TLDR: A little girl vanished beneath a bridge as rain-swollen Hubble Creek swept her into a dangerous culvert. Four boys, including an 11-year-old, joined forces to rescue her. Her mother’s way of thanking them? Free burgers for life.Imagine standing beside a creek after heavy rain, watching water rush over a low bridge. One moment, a little girl is splashing nearby. The next, she is gone. Then, just as panic begins to set in, a hand appears above the water.That was the frightening moment that confronted 11-year-old Aiden Kyle in Jackson, Missouri, on May 17, 2020. Five-year-old Kinsley Stuart had been swept beneath a low-water bridge at Hubble Creek, where a powerful current pulled her into an uncovered drainage culvert. Aiden jumped in and grabbed her, but the force of the water was too strong for him to manage alone.His friends joined him. What followed was a desperate, collective effort that brought Kinsley back to safety. And when her mother, Casey Stuart, tried to find a way to thank the four boys, she offered them something they would never forget: free food at her family’s restaurant for the rest of their lives. The rescue was reported by local broadcaster KFVS12 at the time.The story has resurfaced in an October 2026 Reddit post, attracting renewed attention to a rescue that was about much more than a generous reward.A hand above the water was all Aiden could seeThe creek had risen after heavy rain, turning a familiar place to play into a dangerous stretch of moving water. Children had gathered at Jackson City Park, where water flowed over the low-water bridge.Kinsley was playing nearby when the current swept her towards the culvert beneath the bridge. According to KFVS12, Aiden noticed that she had disappeared and then spotted her hand above the water. He immediately went in to help.“I saw her hand on top of the bridge part, so I jumped in and I grabbed on,” Aiden told the broadcaster.But grabbing hold of Kinsley was only the beginning. The current was powerful enough to pull Aiden towards the culvert as well. His friend Isaiah Randol joined the rescue, and the two struggled to bring the girl out. When they could not manage it alone, Alex Niedbalski and Aiden’s brother, Elias Kyle, also entered the water.“It took four boys to pull this girl out because it was that strong,” Isaiah told KFVS12.Together, the four boys managed to get Kinsley out of the water and to safety. She was taken to Saint Francis Medical Center for examination and was released after being checked, according to reports at the time.The incident is a reminder that the appearance of a creek can be misleading. Water that seems manageable at the surface can move with considerable force after heavy rain. Structures beneath the water, sudden changes in depth and concealed openings can make natural waterways particularly unpredictable.The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that rivers and other natural bodies of water can contain hidden hazards, including dangerous currents, rocks and vegetation. Conditions can change quickly with weather, and drowning can happen in seconds. The agency recommends close supervision of children near water and the use of properly fitted life jackets for children around natural water.The promise that turned gratitude into a lifelong rewardThe day after the rescue, Kinsley's mother, Casey Stuart, reached out to thank the boys. Her family owned Kenny’s Flippin’ Burgers, a restaurant business, and she decided to give them a reward that reflected what they had done.“We do want to say thank you to the boys, from Kenny’s,” she said in the local news report. She then promised that they could eat at the restaurant for free for the rest of their lives.“There is no amount of money that can ever be put on what you did,” she added.The story’s enduring appeal lies not simply in the promise of free food, but in the moment that came before it: an 11-year-old noticing a hand above rushing water, calling for help and being joined by three friends who refused to leave the rescue to him alone.The four boys were children themselves. They did not have professional rescue equipment or the protection of a trained water-rescue team. They saw someone in danger and responded together.Their actions saved Kinsley that day. And the reward her mother offered became a lasting reminder of how one extraordinary act can leave an entire community grateful.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: What is Starshield? SpaceX’s Starlink-based network at the heart of Ukraine’s battlefield crisis
articles.summary: The US has reportedly restricted Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starshield satellite network, disrupting some military drone operations and exposing Kyiv’s
articles.body: The US has reportedly restricted Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starshield satellite network, disrupting some military drone operations and exposing Kyiv’s dependence on American-controlled space technology.The move has drawn attention to Starshield, SpaceX’s national security-focused satellite system, and its role in supporting battlefield communications, drone warfare and air defence against Russian attacks.Starshield is a SpaceX programme that develops satellite systems for government and national security missions, including those of the US military.Unveiled in 2022, it builds on the technology and infrastructure developed for Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet network, but is designed for specialised defence and intelligence requirements.SpaceX identifies three main functions for Starshield: secure communications, Earth observation and hosting specialised payloads on satellites.Its secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, while relying on the wider Starlink satellite constellation as their backbone. The US Department of Defense is its largest customer.The distinction is important in Ukraine, where satellite connectivity has become integral to battlefield communications and drone operations.While Starlink is a commercial service controlled by SpaceX, Elon Musk has said Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, with restrictions on its use determined by the US military and ultimately the president.Why Starshield is important for Ukraine?For Ukraine, satellite connectivity is more than a means of communication. It supports military coordination, drone operations and the transmission of information across a battlefield where conventional communications infrastructure can be damaged or disrupted. Any restrictions on access can therefore affect how Ukrainian forces coordinate operations and respond to Russian attacks.The importance of the network became evident after Ukrainian officials reported that restrictions on satellite connectivity disrupted several drone missions.Reuters reported on October 14 that terminals lost connectivity when moving at speeds above 160 km/h, forcing some Ukrainian units to cancel missions. The restrictions were particularly significant for faster drones used in strikes against Russian logistics and in air defence operations.The disruption also affected frontline communications. In a report published on October 16, Reuters described how an artillery unit in eastern Ukraine experienced interruptions in communications with headquarters and a significant drop in internet speeds after Starlink services were reduced.For Kyiv, therefore, the issue extends beyond internet access. Any sustained disruption could complicate drone operations, weaken battlefield coordination and make it harder for Ukrainian forces to respond to Russian attacks.

articles.title: In 1993, a rancher donated 300 American bison that were released on an Oklahoma prairie; today, more than 2,000 roam the preserve, helping restore one of Earth's most threatened ecosystems
articles.summary: In 1993, Oklahoma ranchers Kenneth and Dianna Adams donated 300 American bison to The Nature Conservancy, setting in motion a conservation effort to
articles.body: In 1993, Oklahoma ranchers Kenneth and Dianna Adams donated 300 American bison to The Nature Conservancy, setting in motion a conservation effort to restore one of North America's most threatened ecosystems. More than three decades later, the herd has grown to thousands of animals roaming the Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve near Pawhuska, Oklahoma. Spanning 39,650 acres, the preserve protects a rare stretch of native grassland where bison grazing and carefully managed fires help maintain the natural balance of the prairie. The animals influence the growth of native plants, create habitats for other species and help preserve the ecological processes that shaped the Great Plains for thousands of years. Their return is particularly significant because less than 4% of the original tallgrass prairie remains.The bison were named the Christina Adams Bison Herd after the ranchers' daughter. Their growing population has become a defining feature of the preserve, where the animals roam across open grassland and graze among native vegetation.The conservation effort also demonstrates how restoring a native species can contribute to the protection of an entire landscape. The preserve supports hundreds of plant and animal species, making the long-term management of its grasslands important for biodiversity.From 300 bison to a herd of thousandsThe original herd arrived in autumn 1993, when the Adams family donated the animals from their Ken-Ada Ranch. The Nature Conservancy had begun assembling the preserve through land acquisitions in 1989, with the goal of protecting and restoring the region's disappearing tallgrass prairie.The herd has since expanded considerably. The Nature Conservancy has reported around 2,700 bison during summer, including calves born that year, with numbers falling after the annual autumn roundup. The animals are managed as part of the preserve's conservation programme, which combines wildlife management with efforts to maintain the grassland's natural character.The preserve covers approximately 39,650 acres and is recognised as the largest protected remnant of tallgrass prairie in the world. Its landscape includes rolling grasslands, native wildflowers, scattered trees and waterways, offering a glimpse of an ecosystem that once covered vast areas of central North America.How bison help restore the grasslandBison play a central role in shaping the prairie through their feeding habits and movement. They primarily graze on grasses, influencing which plants dominate the landscape and creating opportunities for other vegetation to grow. This helps maintain a varied grassland rather than allowing a limited number of plant species to dominate every area.Their activities also affect the soil. As bison move through the preserve, they disturb patches of ground, redistribute nutrients through their waste and create depressions known as wallows by rolling in the soil. These shallow hollows can collect rainwater and provide small habitats for insects and other wildlife.The resulting variation in vegetation and ground conditions supports a wider range of organisms. Native grasses and flowering plants provide food and shelter for insects, while birds and mammals depend on the different habitats found across the prairie.Why controlled fires are essentialBison grazing is combined with prescribed burning, another important tool in tallgrass prairie management. Without periodic disturbance, woody plants can spread into open grasslands, gradually changing the landscape and reducing the habitat available to species adapted to prairie conditions.The Nature Conservancy uses a patch-burn approach, setting controlled fires in different sections of the preserve at different times. Recently burned areas produce fresh vegetation, while other sections retain older grasses and provide different feeding opportunities for wildlife.Bison graze across these contrasting areas, further shaping plant growth and maintaining a changing mosaic of habitats. Together, grazing and fire recreate some of the natural processes that historically sustained the Great Plains, helping keep the preserve an open grassland rather than allowing it to become dominated by shrubs and trees.Research shows how bison can increase plant diversityThe ecological importance of bison is also supported by long-term research at the Konza Prairie Biological Station in Kansas. A study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in August 2022 examined nearly three decades of vegetation data from areas grazed by bison, areas grazed by cattle and areas without large grazers.Researchers found that native plant species richness was 103% higher at the small-plot scale and 86% higher at the larger catchment scale in bison-grazed areas than in ungrazed areas. Cattle grazing also increased plant richness, although the gains were smaller.The research highlighted how grazing by native large herbivores can influence the composition of grassland vegetation over long periods. The study also found that the gains associated with bison grazing persisted through a period that included severe drought, underscoring the importance of grazing patterns in maintaining prairie biodiversity.Protecting one of America's most threatened ecosystemsTallgrass prairie once stretched across 14 US states, extending from Texas to Minnesota and into parts of Canada. Agricultural conversion and urban development have destroyed much of this habitat, leaving less than 4% of its original extent. Much of the remaining prairie is concentrated in Oklahoma and Kansas, particularly in the Flint Hills region.The Joseph H. Williams Tallgrass Prairie Preserve protects a significant part of this surviving landscape. It supports more than 700 plant species, over 300 bird species and around 80 mammal species, according to The Nature Conservancy. Its grasslands provide food, shelter and breeding habitat for wildlife while preserving native vegetation that has disappeared from much of the region.The return of the bison has helped restore a defining feature of the prairie. More than 30 years after the original donation, the herd remains central to the preserve's conservation work, showing how native wildlife and careful land management can help sustain a threatened ecosystem for future generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Costly craze to modify bikes is illegal too
articles.summary: The roar of a high-speed bike, a ‘wheelie’ or ‘stoppie’ on a busy road — behaviour every one of those illegal road stunts is a modified motorcycle
articles.body: The roar of a high-speed bike, a ‘wheelie’ or ‘stoppie’ on a busy road — behaviour every one of those illegal road stunts is a modified motorcycle violating many a clause of the Motor Vehicles Act.Two weeks ago, at least 50 bikers gathered on Valluvar Kottam High Road and performed stunts, including wheelies, stoppies and drifts. Greater Chennai Police tracked and arrested at least 21 of them. All their bikes were ‘modified’, costing several lakhs of rupees.Factory-built motorcycles are calibrated to balance power, torque, fuel efficiency, emissions and safety while complying with Bharat Stage (BS) VI emission norms. However, changes to the exhaust, air intake, and engine settings can alter performance and potentially affect emissions, reliability and safety.Arjun Kumar, a pit stop owner in Pudupet, said, “Customers spend between 18 and 25% more to enhance the engine tuning, though it could affect mileage and engine life if not done properly. Modified bikes are not covered by insurance.”“More than speed or appearance, riders want a bike that reflects their personality and responds differently when they accelerate, brake or take a corner,” said Karthik, a track rider from Coimbatore.However, modifications can cross the line from customisation to violations. Section 52 of the Motor Vehicles Act restricts alterations that make a vehicle’s registration particulars differ from those specified by the manufacturer. Section 190(2) addresses violations of prescribed safety and noise standards.MORE THAN SPEED OR APPEARANCE, RIDERS WANT A BIKE THAT REFLECTS THEIR PERSONALITY AND RESPONDS DIFFERENTLY WHEN THEY ACCELERATE, BRAKE OR TURN A CORNER— R Karthik | A track rider from Coimbatore1. TYRESCost: Rs 10K–Rs 20K (per tyre)What it does: Replaces stock tyres with wider, high-grip tyres.Benefits: Better grip and stability.Improved cornering performance.Enhanced look.Things to keep in mind: Tyre choice affects mileage and fuel efficiency and may require changes to the swingarm or fender in some cases.2. AIR FILTERCost: Rs 2K–Rs 6KWhat it does: Allows more air to flow into the engine.Benefits: Better throttle response.Can slightly increase power output.Things to keep in mind: Requires regular cleaning and maintenance. Gains are limited without other modifications.3. EXHAUSTCost: Rs 10K–Rs 20KWhat it does: Replaces the stock exhaust with a free-flow system.Benefits: Louder and deeper exhaust note.Reduced weight.Can improve exhaust flow and power when tuned properly.Things to keep in mind: Excessive noise may lead to legal violations.4. CUSTOM PAINTCost: Rs 5K–Rs 25KWhat it does: Changes the bike’s appearance with custom paint, wraps or graphics.Benefits: Unique and personalised look.Wide range of design options.Things to keep in mind: Keep modifications within legal requirements. Cost varies based on paint quality, design complexity and finish.5. ECU TUNINGCost: Rs 8K–Rs 22KWhat it does: Reprograms the bike’s engine control unit (ECU) to adjust fuel injection and other parameters.Benefits: Improved throttle response.Better power delivery.Can unlock additional performance when combined with other modifications.Things to keep in mind: Incorrect tuning can reduce engine life and affect reliability.6. SUSPENSION UPGRADECost: Rs 15K–Rs 40KWhat it does: Replaces or enhances the stock suspension (front/rear).Benefits: Better handling and stability.Improved ride quality.More control at high speeds.Things to keep in mind: Cost varies based on brand and type, such as adjustable suspension.7. articles.title: McClellan Air Force Base closed in 2001; 25 years later, the 3,000-acre Sacramento site has drawn about $600 million in investment, with 10 million sq ft of buildings and a public-use airport
articles.summary: When McClellan Air Force Base closed in July 2001, the decision threatened thousands of jobs and raised concerns about the economic future of the
articles.body: When McClellan Air Force Base closed in July 2001, the decision threatened thousands of jobs and raised concerns about the economic future of the surrounding Sacramento community. A quarter-century later, the former military installation has become McClellan Park, a business and industrial hub with around $600 million in investment, 10 million square feet of buildings and a public-use airport. According to the U.S. Air Force Civil Engineer Center (AFCEC), the redevelopment has involved partnerships between the Air Force, Sacramento County and private developers, alongside environmental restoration. A 2020 McClellan Park fact sheet documents the scale of investment and the site's transformation into a centre for businesses, transport and community services.From military installation to commercial centreMcClellan Air Force Base was once one of the Sacramento region's major employers. The base supported military logistics and maintenance operations for more than six decades, employing thousands of military and civilian workers. Its closure was announced in 1995 under the federal Base Realignment and Closure process. The decision was expected to cost the local economy thousands of jobs and disrupt businesses that depended on the installation. Before the base officially closed, private businesses were brought into vacant buildings through a process known as a “hot transfer”. This helped retain some employment and allowed redevelopment to begin before the closure, according to McClellan Park’s historical account.$600 million investment and millions of square feetThe scale of the redevelopment is reflected in the site's infrastructure and commercial activity. McClellan Park's 2020 fact sheet records approximately $600 million in total economic investment, 10 million square feet of buildings and an occupancy rate of 90%. The site accommodates a mix of private businesses, government agencies, industrial facilities, offices and community organisations. Its large buildings have been adapted for different uses, allowing existing structures to serve new commercial purposes instead of requiring every business to start with new construction.The park's development potential also extends beyond its existing buildings. The 2020 fact sheet identifies another five million square feet of potential development, indicating that the property still had room to expand. The same document estimates that the site attracts between 15,000 and 17,000 daily visitors. These figures illustrate how a former military installation has become a major employment and business destination for the surrounding region.A military airport becomes a public-use facilityOne of the most significant changes has been the conversion of the former military airport into a public-use airport serving general aviation. According to McClellan Park's fact sheet, the airport has a 10,600-foot runway. The property also contains seven miles of on-site railway connected directly to Union Pacific and BNSF rail lines, providing transport infrastructure alongside its commercial and industrial facilities.Former military buildings have found new purposes, too. The Air Force officers' club became The Officer's Club restaurant, while the former fitness centre now houses California Family Fitness. A former bowling alley has been converted into a classroom and learning centre operated by Gateway Community Charters. These adaptations demonstrate how existing facilities can support civilian businesses, education, recreation and public services after a military installation closes.Environmental cleanup remains part of the transformationThe redevelopment has required more than attracting businesses and renovating buildings. Past military operations, waste disposal and chemical spills left soil and groundwater contamination that needed to be addressed.The Air Force has continued environmental restoration alongside the property's transition to civilian use. In 2007, the Air Force and Sacramento County established an agreement designed to accelerate cleanup and allow land to be transferred for redevelopment sooner. The arrangement brought together government agencies, environmental regulators and the private developer. The Air Force Civil Engineer Center reported in 2018 that McClellan's restoration programme had involved 325 sites requiring investigation. Cleanup measures included groundwater treatment, soil remediation and protective caps over contaminated areas. The project also received a US Environmental Protection Agency award recognising efforts to restore former federal facilities for productive reuse.McClellan Park's transformation illustrates how a closed military base can become a long-term economic asset when redevelopment, infrastructure investment and environmental restoration proceed together. Twenty-five years after the base shut down, the Sacramento site continues to serve businesses and the public while demonstrating a different future for land once dedicated to military operations.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘He spoke to Putin to buy diesel’: Ex-diplomat Fabian after Trump waives sanctions over Russian oil
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former diplomat KP Fabian on Saturday questioned the rationale behind the US tariff pressure on India over Russian oil purchases, arguing that
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former diplomat KP Fabian on Saturday questioned the rationale behind the US tariff pressure on India over Russian oil purchases, arguing that Washington’s own decision to waive sanctions-related duties under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act exposed a contradiction in its approach.His remarks came after US President Donald Trump earlier today waived sanctions-related duties under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.Speaking to ANI, Fabian said, “Trump himself spoke to Putin to buy diesel. If America itself is buying, either it should sanction itself, which is ridiculous."He also argued that the tariff threats against India were a negotiating tactic aimed at securing a favourable trade deal rather than a genuine response to New Delhi’s energy purchases from Russia.“Certain tariffs were imposed, and the court in the United States said that Trump had no business."Fabian said Trump had avoided directly confronting Chinese President Xi Jinping over Russian oil purchases because China was a major buyer of Russian exports and Washington wanted closer engagement with Beijing.“Contrary to the Lindsey Graham Act, President Trump did not dare to mention it to Xi Jinping because China is a top buyer, 50 per cent of Russia’s exports. India comes next at 37 per cent,” he told ANI.Trump pauses sanctionsHowever, Trump earlier on Saturday paused provisions of the Graham Act that could have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported into the US from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, including India and China.The move comes against the backdrop of rising diesel prices in the US ahead of the November midterm elections and a reported agreement under which Russia would supply diesel fuel to Washington.Trump invoked Section 115 of the Act, which authorises the US president to waive certain sanctions-related provisions and restrictions involving foreign entities.“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order.What it means for IndiaRussia continues to be the single largest supplier of oil for India. A waiver of tariffs of up to 100% which may have come into place in the coming days means that India can continue importing oil in large numbers from Moscow without any economic fallout.If 100% tariffs had been imposed by the Trump administration, then it would have hit exporters as the US is the largest trading partner for India. At the same time, any sanctions may have rendered Russian crude economically unviable which would have added to the supply crunch at a time when Middle East tensions continue.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: NAGPUR: An attempt to terminate an advanced pregnancy using YouTube videos and herbal concoctions ended with a 16-year-old girl delivering a baby at home,
articles.body: NAGPUR: An attempt to terminate an advanced pregnancy using YouTube videos and herbal concoctions ended with a 16-year-old girl delivering a baby at home, after which her 18-year-old classmate was arrested and charged with rape.The girl had allegedly been made to consume herbal concoctions and abortion medicines for several weeks after informing the youth that she was pregnant. Instead of seeking medical assistance, the boy allegedly watched YouTube videos to find ways to terminate the pregnancy. The attempt failed, and the girl went into labour on Monday.Her condition deteriorated after the delivery, prompting her family to rush her to a government-run hospital early this week. The newborn was taken to a private hospital. Doctors at Government Medical College and Hospital (GMCH) alerted police after the girl developed severe post-delivery complications.According to Pachpaoli police, the accused and the survivor studied at the same school in north Nagpur. They allegedly became intimate last year at the boy’s residence when his family members were away. He continued to have physical relations with her and had also promised to marry her, police said.Police recorded the survivor’s statement and registered a rape FIR on Thursday under relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act.Senior Inspector Jeetendra Bobde of Pachpaoli police station said the accused may have recently turned 18, but was a minor at the time of the first alleged sexual encounter. His age at the time of the alleged offence would be examined to determine the applicable legal procedure.Police are completing the legal formalities and will ensure the survivor receives counselling and psychological support, senior PI Bobde said, adding that the case would be referred to the child welfare committee.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Nagpur | Silver Rate in Nagpur | Bank Holidays in Nagpur | Public Holidays in Nagpur | Petrol Price in Nagpur | Diesel Price in Nagpur | CNG Price in Nagpur | LPG Price in NagpurStay updated with the latest Nagpur news.
